# If AI takes every job who will buy things?

The answer is worse than you think.

The big tech CEOs keep saying AI will replace 100% of jobs.

There is one big problem, though: if AI replaces every job, how will people buy things?

Pro-AI accelerationists say we will get universal basic income (UBI). They think the government will give everyone enough money each month to cover basic living expenses.

One of the main problems with this idea is that politicians in the U.S. aren’t taking it seriously or working toward it in any meaningful way, so I’m not optimistic we’ll get it anytime soon.

I think we are much more likely to see AI improving productivity, fewer companies hiring, and more and more people falling through the cracks, unable to get a job, and forced to survive however they can while permanently locked out of the job market.

This is especially likely if AI plays out how I think it will.

I don’t believe in the recursive self-improvement-leading-to-superintelligence hype. If things play out the way the most bullish AI researchers keep suggesting, we will have superintelligence that can do every job in the world better than any human could in 6 months.

In that scenario, UBI is more likely because it would happen all at once. If superintelligence arrived in 2027 and was better than humans at every single white-collar job and companies started firing their entire staff and replacing them with AI en masse, the government would have to intervene with something like UBI or risk the entire economy collapsing.

What I think is more likely is that AI will significantly affect unemployment, but it will happen slowly, and people will be left to figure it out themselves. Slow is worse, because nobody is forced to act.

So who will buy things? Fewer and fewer people. The economy won’t collapse overnight. Spending will just slowly concentrate in the hands of the people who still have money coming in. This is already happening with the K-shaped economy where the top 20% of income earners drive nearly 60% of spending. Since the pandemic, the bottom 80% have barely grown their spending faster than inflation.

In this scenario, AI will automate almost all execution, like building websites, running ads, sending cold emails, etc while humans still make judgment decisions like what products to sell and how to position them.

In a world like that, the winners will be founders who own companies and benefit from the automation, and employees with great judgment who use AI to get outsized results.

The jobs that are doing well right now support that view.

Software engineering jobs are flat, but product managers are in huge demand. According to Lenny Rachitsky’s latest job market report , open PM roles are up 75% from their 2023 low, the highest they’ve been in nearly four years.

And the PMs companies want are technical. Two years ago, the most mentioned skills in PM job descriptions were SQL, Jira, AWS, and Python. Today, the number one skill is “LLM.” Claude is number three, and Cursor, MCP, and evals are all in the top ten. AI-focused PMs now make $245,000 compared to $123,000 for traditional PMs.

AI is taking over execution, like writing code, and companies are paying a premium for people who have the judgment to decide what to build and know enough about AI to direct it.

Hopefully, we will get UBI at some point, but the people who aren’t building any skills, assuming we will get it, are going to be in enormous trouble if superintelligence ends up not happening quickly.

The skill I’m betting on is running my work through AI. I do it with a second brain I built and Claude Duet, which helps me manage my content system that gets ten million views a month on social media.
